name: Kira Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor in the commercial property team at a regional firm, and my clients are mostly family businesses: shops, restaurants, a couple of small factories. A normal day is drafting and checking leases, answering landlords who want the rent review sorted, and phoning shop owners to explain what a break clause is, which means the date they're allowed to leave the lease early. I like the clients, because they're like my own family, people who built something from nothing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Long leases, sixty pages, where I miss a clause and Mrs Adeyemi, my supervisor, finds it in five minutes. I'm still learning, and I know it. I use the firm's AI drafting tool sometimes, once Mrs Adeyemi showed us how, mostly to compare two versions of a lease. At home, my husband Hao runs his family's restaurant with his parents, and we're saving for a deposit on a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper for comparing documents and that's fine. Hard work and good judgement still matter most. I'd say that at work and to Hao's parents, who never trusted any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's fine, but our money isn't as steady as it looks. The restaurant has thin margins, food prices went up again, and some months Hao takes home almost nothing. My salary is the reliable one, and we've only got about three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I do and ask Mrs Adeyemi for more lease drafting, so I stop missing clauses. I'd keep using the drafting tool for comparisons, maybe a few times a week. And we'd keep putting £300 a month towards the deposit, and less if the restaurant has a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, more about the restaurant and whether we'll ever have our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a bad month at the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hao's parents don't take their wages, and Hao takes less, and I pay the rent. In a bad month at my husband's family restaurant, my lawyer's salary pays everyone's rent. Nobody says it, but we all know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our team secretary, Brenda, who formats all the leases. If even the simple tools do the formatting, the firm might cut her hours. She's been there twenty years, and she's the one who knows where every old deed is kept.

say: AI is a **useful helper** for comparing documents.
**Hard work** and **good judgement** still matter most.
I'd say it to Hao's parents, who **never trusted** any of it.

fieldNote: Her worry in a no-change world is the **restaurant's thin margins**, not AI.

She values **hard work** and family support over outside help.

steps.text: Ask for more lease drafting work to improve
Use the firm's AI tool to compare lease versions
Save £300 a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every business has to keep up, law firms and restaurants alike. I wouldn't complain about it, because complaining doesn't pay the rent. I'd tell the family business clients to use the tools for their bookings and orders too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of my lease work moves to software. Drafting, checking and comparing are right on that card. The firm would need fewer juniors, and I'm not the best one, so I could see myself on a short list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the firm's AI training properly, after the first group had been through it and said it helps. I'd try to become the person family-business clients ask for, because I understand how they think. And I'd help Hao set up online booking and ordering at the restaurant, which might save his mum an hour a day on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. I'd keep busy, which is how my family deals with worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be on the short list. What would you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at smaller firms in town, there are a few. Or I'd go in-house at a company that owns a lot of shops. I wouldn't wait for the government to save my job. I'd go knocking on doors at every shop in town before I'd ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Hao's parents see the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His dad would say computers can't cook, which is true, for now. His mum would quietly start using the booking system and never admit it helped. They'd want us to keep both incomes, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to pull together, and businesses should be free to adapt. I wouldn't call for big handouts. I'd say people should help each other find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job goes. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, drafting leases is gone first. The restaurant would be safer for a few years, because cooking and serving are hands-on, and robots come about three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Hao and his parents about me joining the restaurant, doing the books, the suppliers, the contracts, and maybe opening a takeaway counter. We'd put the deposit savings into the restaurant instead of a flat. And I'd move us in with Hao's parents above the restaurant to cut rent, which they've offered before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And a bit embarrassed, because I'd be the lawyer who ended up working in the family shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the restaurant is our lifeboat until about 2031. My husband's family restaurant would be our lifeboat until the cooking robots arrive, around 2031. After that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own rent, by moving in above the restaurant. Then the car, because I'd be walking to work downstairs. The last thing to go would be the money we send to my grandmother.

say: Families and communities need to **pull together**.
Businesses should be **free to adapt**, without big **handouts**.
People should **help each other** find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people who work hard to find their place. I'd tell my clients to plan ahead, and I'd do the same. I'd keep it positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is useful. I'd keep my job for maybe three years and build the restaurant side at the same time. By 2031 I'd want one foot in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, £300 a month, but into a business account rather than the flat deposit. I'd do the restaurant's contracts and supplier deals for free in the evenings, to learn it. And around year two I'd do a short course on running a small food business, maybe £500.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than in the two-year picture. I'd have a plan with dates in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about children in two years. We'd probably still try, because Hao's mum would help with childcare. In my family, grandparents raise the children while the parents work. That's how my husband Hao was raised, and how we'd raise ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't blame anyone, really. Businesses do what makes money; that's how it works. I'd only be cross with people who saw it coming and didn't prepare, including me.

Clients should **plan ahead**, and so should I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and people should use it to build something of their own. I'd keep working hard at the firm. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job looks okay for the next few years. By 2036 I'd be 37, and I'd want to be a senior lawyer or running the restaurant's second branch, ideally both. The worry is there, but it's far enough away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and use the AI tools more as they improve. We'd buy the flat in about three years as planned. And I'd keep helping with the restaurant's paperwork, so I'm ready if I need to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but it doesn't stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you switch earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my firm stopped hiring trainees, or if Mrs Adeyemi told me to look elsewhere. She'd tell me straight, she's like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about choosing a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A law degree is good, but owning something is better. I'd tell my children to learn a skill and help in the family business. That's what Hao's parents taught me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd lose my job just as we were about to buy a flat. What would help is cheap loans for small family businesses and apprenticeships for adults who want to switch. I don't want a cheque from the government; I want a fair chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about families who work together. I don't want a cheque from the government. I want a fair chance to work, and a family business that can still pay its bills.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque from the government. I want a fair chance to work, and a family business that can still pay its bills.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** commercial property junior whose clients are **family businesses**.
Her husband runs his family's **restaurant**, and her salary is the **steady income**.
She uses AI **once it's proven** and would bring it into the restaurant too.
As AGI nears she moves **into the restaurant**, which gets about three extra hands-on years.
She values **self-reliance** and family, and blames no one for market change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, just as they were about to buy a flat.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for adults who want to switch careers.
